overview: Investment fund managers decide where a fund's money goes: which stocks, bonds or other assets to buy, when to sell and how much risk to take. They track performance, study markets and explain results to clients. O*NET rates their enterprising interest at 6.95 out of 7 and knowledge of economics and accounting at 4.67 out of 5. Most hold a bachelor's or master's degree, plus years of analyst experience. BLS reports pay only for the broader financial managers group, with a median of $166,570. Expect long hours at a desk and tight deadlines when markets move.
pay: BLS does not publish pay for fund managers alone, so these figures are for the broader financial managers group. Its median is $166,570, and the top 10% earn $323,270 or more, before bonuses tied to fund returns. New York has the highest state median at $219,880, 32% above the national figure.

faq.q: How much do investment fund managers make?
faq.a: BLS reports pay for the broader financial managers group: a May 2025 median of $166,570 and a top 10% at $323,270 or more. Fund managers often earn bonuses on top, so total pay varies widely. New York ($219,880), Massachusetts ($206,760) and New Jersey ($199,110) have the highest state medians.

faq.q: What education do investment fund managers need?
faq.a: In O*NET data, 63% of fund managers hold a master's degree and 33% a bachelor's degree. There are 11 related majors, including finance, accounting and financial analytics. Most also spend several years as analysts and earn professional credentials before managing money for clients.

faq.q: What skills do fund managers need?
faq.a: O*NET rates critical thinking, reading comprehension and active listening at 4 out of 5 for this job. Knowledge of economics and accounting is rated 4.67 and mathematics 4.34. You also need to explain decisions clearly to clients, since speaking is rated 3.88.

faq.q: What jobs are similar to investment fund manager?
faq.a: The closest matches are securities and financial services sales agents (92%), Personal Financial Advisors (90%) and Financial Quantitative Analysts (87%), based on O*NET 31.0. Personal Financial Advisors earn a median of $105,070 and work directly with individual clients rather than funds.
